frames.narration: Release 412 ships. GET /orders p50 goes from 40 ms to 80 ms and CPU per request from 1.0 ms to 2.0 ms. Metrics and traces say this service is slow, not which code.
Turn on a sampling profiler at 100 Hz. Every 10 ms a timer interrupts the process and the profiler records the current call stack. No call or return is traced.
Identical stacks are counted. After 60 s there are 6,000 samples, and handler;serialize;json_encode;encode_loop appears in about 3,510 of them (58.5%).
The store merges the stacks into a tree and the viewer draws it: root at the bottom, callees on top, width = share of samples. The x axis is not time; siblings are sorted alphabetically.

Read it by self vs total. serialize is 65.5% total but only 2.5% self: it is wide because of its callee. The wide plateau on top, encode_loop (58.5% self), is where the CPU goes. Tall narrow towers cost little.

A differential flame graph against last week's profile: encode_loop went from 170 to 1,170 microseconds per request (+1,000), every other function is unchanged. That is the whole regression, an accidental O(n^2) loop.

Caveat: this was a CPU profile. Per request the wall time is about 5.6 ms: 2.0 ms on CPU, 3.0 ms waiting on the database socket, 0.6 ms on a mutex. Only a wall-clock (off-CPU) profile shows those waits.

Replace the linear search with a set and deploy. The always-on profiler (100 Hz, about 1% CPU) shows encode_loop back at 17% of a 1.0 ms request, and the profile of the new version is stored for next time.
